name: Sermorelin
summary: A shortened copy of the brain hormone that tells the pituitary to release growth hormone; once an approved drug, now compounded and used to raise growth hormone and IGF-1.
what_it_is: Sermorelin is a lab-made peptide that matches the active first part (amino acids 1-29) of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), which the brain uses to signal the pituitary gland. It prompts the pituitary to release the body's own growth hormone, which in turn raises IGF-1. It was sold in the US as Geref, for testing pituitary function and for children with growth hormone deficiency, until the maker stopped selling it in 2008.

evidence.why: It was an approved drug for children with growth hormone deficiency, but evidence for the adult uses people seek today (body composition, aging) found here is limited to a small retrospective study and reviews.

status_us.label: Compounded by prescription; former approved drug
status_us.note: Approved as Geref in 1990 (pituitary test) and 1997 (children with growth hormone deficiency); FDA withdrew the approvals in 2009 after the maker stopped selling it, and later found this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. FDA lists sermorelin acetate as a component of an approved drug, which allows pharmacy compounding by prescription; WADA bans it in sport.

benefits.claim: Triggers growth hormone release from the pituitary; FDA approved it as a test of the pituitary's ability to make growth hormone
Treated growth failure in children with idiopathic growth hormone deficiency (its approved use, 1997-2009), though a 2012 review called it largely ineffective as a growth promoter
Raised IGF-1 in 14 men on testosterone therapy who took it together with GHRP-2 and GHRP-6

risks.risk: Compounded versions are not FDA-approved, and FDA does not check their safety, quality or strength before sale
Fluid retention, joint pain, injection-site reactions and higher blood sugar are label warnings for tesamorelin, a drug that works the same way
Long-term safety, including any cancer risk from raising growth hormone and IGF-1, has not been studied

avoid_if: Diabetes or prediabetes (clinician first: drugs that raise growth hormone can raise blood sugar)
Competitive athletes (prohibited by WADA at all times)
interactions: Glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., for adrenal insufficiency): raising growth hormone can increase steroid needs, per the tesamorelin label
Drugs cleared by liver CYP450 enzymes (e.g., anticonvulsants, cyclosporine, sex steroids): growth hormone can change their clearance, per the tesamorelin label

labs.why: No sermorelin-specific guideline exists; the tesamorelin label and a review of growth hormone secretagogues advise checking IGF-1 and blood sugar because these drugs raise IGF-1 and can raise glucose.

studies.title: Growth Hormone Secretagogue Treatment in Hypogonadal Men Raises Serum Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1 Levels
studies.people: 14 men on testosterone therapy (retrospective chart review)
studies.finding: A combination of sermorelin, GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 raised average IGF-1 from about 160 to 239 ng/mL. Body composition could not be assessed and side effects were not systematically recorded.

studies.title: Growth Hormone Doping in Sports: A Critical Review of Use and Detection Strategies
studies.finding: Describes sermorelin as marketed for children with growth hormone deficiency and for pituitary testing, largely ineffective as a growth promoter, and no longer sold in the US.

ask_your_clinician: Is my IGF-1 actually low, and what result would show this is working?
Which pharmacy would compound it, and how is its quality checked?
Given my blood sugar and cancer screening history, is a drug that raises growth hormone safe for me?

notes_for_editor: The web-search budget ran out before the older-adult trials could be opened (the prototype cited Corpas 1992 and Vittone 1997 on GH/IGF-1 and body composition in men over 60); add them only after checking. The Geref label was not found, so class risks and interactions are borrowed from the tesamorelin label and flagged as such. Conflict: FDA approved sermorelin for pediatric growth hormone deficiency, yet the 2012 Endocrine Reviews article calls it largely ineffective as a growth promoter; graded moderate. Compounding status is inferred from FDA's 503B list marking sermorelin acetate as a component of an approved drug plus the 503A rule allowing such components; no 2025-2026 FDA action on sermorelin could be checked. Source 9 (secretagogue review) supports the IGF-1/glucose monitoring advice in labs.
